blocks.x: COM SKILLS 157 · Communication Skills · Topic 4

Concord means agreement — between two units in a sentence in terms of number, person and gender. It is one of the most heavily tested areas of English grammar at KNUST because it quietly governs almost every sentence you write: get the subject and verb out of step, and the sentence sounds wrong even when every individual word is spelled correctly.

By the end of this module, you will be able to…

items: 1Define concord and explain why English grammar requires agreement between related units of a sentence in number, person and gender.

2Identify the different types of concord — gender, number, tense-harmony, determiner-noun, adjunct/adverbial-verb, object-complement, subject-complement, verb-object and subject-verb concord — in real Ghanaian-English sentences.
3Distinguish notional, situational/pragmatic and grammatical concord, and apply each correctly to collective nouns, words that are plural in form, and zero-plural nouns.
4Apply the core subject-verb concord rules (SS:SV, PS:PV), correctly identify singular and plural subjects, and resolve agreement in sentences joined by and or by correlative and pseudo-conjunctions.
5Handle harder cases — relative clauses, complex subjects, ‘a number of’ vs ‘the number of’, indefinite pronouns — and diagnose and correct common concord errors.

blocks.x: Key definitions

Concord Agreement. In English grammar, concord is the agreement between two units in a sentence in terms of number (singular/plural), person (1st/2nd/3rd) and gender (masculine/feminine/neuter). The biblical epigraph often used to open this topic makes the point memorably: “Can two walk together, except they agree?” (Amos 3:3) — two grammatical units cannot sensibly travel together in a sentence unless they agree.

Worked example — Gender concord “The headmaster, who knew what must be done concerning the development of the school, asked the PTA to rally behind him to help realize the dreams of the school.” There is agreement between the noun headmaster and the pronoun him in terms of gender — a textbook example of noun-pronoun concord.

Notional, Situational and Grammatical concord — one-line summary Notional concord depends on the user of the language (the speaker's intended meaning). Situational/pragmatic concord depends on the context of use. Grammatical concord depends on rules — objective markers of singularity and plurality.
Opening diagnostic sentences — spot the concord type
Each sentence below illustrates a different type of concord. Read each one, notice the correction in brackets, and name the concord type — you will meet all of these types again across this topic.

c: One of the alumnae told the students that she would support them.
Universities in Ghana must endeavour to help the communities that surround them (not “it”).
The MP for one of the newly created constituencies promised that she would (not “will”) never disappoint her constituents.
Verb–Verb Concord (Sequence of Tenses / Tense Harmony)
A lot of the phenomena (not “phenomenon”) discussed in textbooks in Ghana are alien to the students.
Two years ago, many students of one of the renowned universities in Ghana obtained (not “obtain”) scholarships for their doctoral studies.
Because they were aware of Dr. Goodworks' potentials, they appointed him president of the association.
The Honourable Minister is the chairperson of the Ghana Peacelovers Union.
The lecturer instructed the course representative to share a book to the students.
The chief of the town champions developmental programmes in his traditional area.

blocks.x: How the three forms of concord relate

Notional Concord
(meaning – user's intention)→ Situational / Pragmatic Concord
(context of use)→ Grammatical Concord
(objective rules & markers)
Three ways a subject can decide its verb

Not every subject-verb pairing is decided the same way. Sometimes meaning wins over form, sometimes context decides, and sometimes it really is just a rule. Knowing which form applies to a given noun is the single most useful skill in this whole topic.
Notional concord

Notional concord (notional agreement) Applying subject-verb agreement according to the intended meaning of the noun rather than to its grammatical form. The verb agrees with the subject based on semantics, not shape — which makes it subjective, because the number of the subject is really decided by what the speaker intends to communicate.

items: 1Collective nouns such as team and committee — grammatically singular in form, but they can take a singular or plural verb depending on whether the group is being thought of as one unit or as many individual members.
2Quantifying pronouns such as all, none, etc. — their number shifts with what they are understood to refer to.

blocks.x: Worked example “The committee are discussing a tight budget.” Here committee takes a plural verb because the speaker is thinking of the committee as a collection of individual members debating among themselves, not as one indivisible body.
Situational / pragmatic agreement

Situational / pragmatic concord The number of the subject is determined by the context (co-text) in which it occurs. Subject-verb agreement rules are applied according to the situation the subject appears in — the same noun can be singular in one sentence and plural in another.

Two classes of nouns behave this way: nouns that are “plural in form” (they end in -s but may take a singular or plural verb depending on meaning), and “zero-plural” nouns, which do not change their form between singular and plural at all — e.g. series, aircraft, species.

The “-ics” rule Words ending in -ics are singular when they refer to a principle, a system, or a field of study (they take a singular verb). When the same word refers to individual practices, applications or activities, it generally takes a plural verb.
Words plural in form vs. zero-plural nouns
Words plural in form (mostly -ics)

News · Statistics · Physics · Ethics · Measles · Calculus · Billiards · Dizziness · Aerodynamics · Mechanics · Aerobics · Series · Economics · Mathematics · Politics · Mumps · Rickets · Molasses · Electronics · Thermodynamics · Aesthetics · Calisthenics
Zero-plural nouns
Information · Furniture · Salmon · Sheep · Grouse · Series · Aircraft · Species
These nouns do not change their spelling between singular and plural — the verb (and context) tells you which one is meant.
Statistics: singular or plural?

c: Statistics is a required course for doctoral students.
Refers to the field of study.
Refers to a specific set of data/figures.
Field of study again, not individual figures.
Statistics show that divorce is a common practice in our society.
Multiple pieces of data about divorce, not the subject as a discipline.

blocks.x: Grammatical concord

Grammatical concord The agreement between a subject and a verb in terms of number, based on the presence or absence of clear formal markers of singularity and plurality (like the ‘s’ ending). This is objective — unlike notional concord, it does not depend on the speaker's intention, it depends on rule-governed markers. This is the form of concord the rest of this topic mostly deals with.

blocks.title: Summary: how the three forms differ

items: Notional concord depends on the user of the language — their intended meaning (e.g. is the committee acting as one body or many members?).
Situational/pragmatic concord depends on the context of use — the same “-ics” word can be singular (field of study) or plural (individual data/activities) depending on the sentence.
Grammatical concord depends on rules — objective singular/plural markers, independent of meaning or context. This is the form tested by the SS:SV / PS:PV rules in the next tab.

sections.title: Important things to note about S-V concord

blocks.x: The engine room of grammatical concord

Grammatical concord runs on a small set of markers and a small set of rules. Master these and you can correct almost any subject-verb disagreement you meet — including the trickiest KNUST exam sentences.
Important things to note about S-V concord

items: 1S-V concord applies to verbs in the present tense — except the verb to be (am, is, are), which also has past-tense concord markers, e.g. He was; They were.
2Only third-person pronouns matter for S-V concord — that is, it, he, she (and their plural equivalent, they). First- and second-person pronouns (I, you, we) do not take the singular ‘s’ marker.
3The subject usually comes before the verb, but not always — sometimes the verb comes before the subject. E.g. “In the room are (plural verb) the boys (plural subject).”
4In S-V disagreement, the correction is done backwards — you first find the subject, establish its number, then adjust the verb to match it (not the other way round).
5Only the SUBJECT affects the verb. Nothing else in the sentence — not the object, not an intervening phrase — has any bearing on whether the verb is singular or plural.

blocks.x: SS:SV and PS:PV
Rule 1 — SS : SV
A singular subject requires a singular verb. The Doctor (singular subject) acts (singular verb) professionally.
Rule 2 — PS : PV
A plural subject requires a plural verb. Serious students (plural subject) admire (plural verb) disciplined teachers.
Units that can function as subject

items: 1Noun phrases: The students are brilliant.
2Pronouns: They understand summum bonum.
3Nominal adjectives (adjectives functioning as nouns): The rich are always happy.
4Nominal clauses (a whole clause functioning as the subject): What he said is true.

blocks.x: The category of number Number is the functional opposition of two forms of the noun: singular (a single referent, e.g. I have a book) or plural (a group referent of two or more members, e.g. She has five books). This singular/plural opposition is characteristic of countable nouns only — uncountable nouns do not switch number this way.
Defining singular and plural subjects & verbs

‘S’ as a plural marker (on nouns) Whenever the plural marker ‘s’ (or ‘es’, or another irregular variant) is added to a noun, the noun becomes plural. A noun carrying this marker, used as a subject, becomes a plural subject (PS). A subject without the plural marker ‘s’ is a singular subject (SS). The country belongs to all. (singular subject) | The books are affordable. (plural subject)

‘S’ as a singular marker (on verbs) This is the mirror image on the verb: any verb without the singular marker ‘s’ (or its variant ‘es’) is a plural verb (e.g. pray, sing, counsel). A verb with the singular marker ‘s’ is a singular verb (e.g. prays, sings, counsels).
When does subject-verb disagreement occur?
Because the noun's ‘s’ marks plural and the verb's ‘s’ marks singular, the two markers work in opposite directions. Disagreement happens in exactly two situations:

c: Both singular and plural markers are present
The students (plural marker) visits (singular marker) the library everyday.
Both singular and plural markers are absent

blocks.x: The guiding principle “One at a time.” A correct sentence carries exactly one ‘s’ marker between the subject and the verb — either on the noun (plural subject, verb has no ‘s’) or on the verb (singular subject, verb has ‘s’) — never both, and never neither.

blocks.title: A student's question: “God bless you” or “God blesses you”?

items: “God bless you” is not a present-tense statement of fact — it is a subjunctive/optative expression (a wish or blessing: “May God bless you”), so the ordinary S-V agreement rule for indicative statements does not apply in the same way.
If you were making a plain indicative statement of present fact about a singular subject (God), grammatical concord would indeed require the singular verb form “God blesses you.”
This is a useful reminder that concord rules are written for ordinary indicative sentences — fixed expressions, wishes and formulaic phrases can look like exceptions.

blocks.x: When two subjects become one — or don't

Joining words look simple, but each family of connector — and, correlative pairs like either...or, and pseudo-conjunctions like as well as — has its own agreement rule, and two of them point the verb in opposite directions.
The basic principle for ‘and’

Basic rule When AND is used to join elements that jointly refer to one unit, the structure selects a singular verb. AND does not automatically make a subject plural — it depends on whether the joined elements are conceptually one thing or genuinely separate things.
When AND still takes a singular verb

items: AMeals treated as one dish: when AND connects two or more entities that together refer to a single meal, the structure is singular. Rice AND soup with elephant meat is delicious.

BNames/titles of a single entity (a company, a book, an organisation): when AND is used inside the name of one entity, the structure is singular. Heaven AND Haven Company Limited deals in building materials.

CTwo singular countable nouns sharing ONE determiner: when AND connects two or more singular countable nouns under a single determiner, the structure is singular. The banker and teacher is approachable. (one person, both banker and teacher) Contrast: The banker and the teacher are approachable. (two separate people, two determiners)
DSynonyms joined by AND: when AND connects words that are near-synonyms expressing one idea, the structure is singular. Power and might belongs to God.

blocks.x: neither…nor / either…or / not only…but also / whether…or

Correlative (compound) conjunctions A class of paired connectors — neither…nor, either…or, not only…but also, whether…or — that connect two or more structures which together function as the subject of a sentence.
Proximity Concord Rule When a correlative conjunction joins a singular and a plural structure, the verb agrees with the noun phrase closest to it (i.e. the one nearer the verb) — proximity decides.

c: Not only the teacher (singular) but also his students (plural) … the motto of the school.
Either the students (NP1) or the lecturer (NP2) … French.

blocks.x: along with, as well as, in addition to… and Remote Concord

Pseudo / quasi / false conjunctions Phrases that look like connectors joining two subjects but grammatically are not true coordinating conjunctions: along with, rather than, with, plus, as well as, in conjunction with, in collaboration with, in addition to, and similar expressions.

Remote Concord Rule Whenever a pseudo-conjunction connects two noun phrases, the verb agrees with the NP that is FAR from the pseudo-conjunction (i.e. the first, main NP) — the opposite of proximity concord. This is why it is called remote concord.

c: The teachers as well as the School Prefect … every term.
The students (NP1) as well as the lecturer (NP2) … French.

blocks.x: Proximity vs. Remote — the crucial contrast
These two rules point in opposite directions, and mixing them up is one of the most common concord errors at this level:
Correlative conjunctions → Proximity
neither…nor, either…or, not only…but also, whether…or → verb agrees with the NP closest to it. Not only the teacher but also his students understand the motto.
Pseudo-conjunctions → Remote
as well as, along with, in addition to, etc. → verb agrees with the NP far from it (the main/first NP). The students as well as the lecturer speak French.

items: Either the students or the lecturer speaks French. → correlative conjunction (either…or) → proximity concord: verb agrees with “the lecturer,” the nearer NP.

The students as well as the lecturer speak French. → pseudo-conjunction (as well as) → remote concord: verb agrees with “the students,” the far NP, even though “the lecturer” sits right next to the verb.
The two sentences contain almost the same words in almost the same order, yet the connector alone flips which rule applies — always identify the connector type first.

blocks.x: The trickiest concord territory

Long, embedded subjects — relative clauses, headword-plus-modifiers structures, quantifying expressions — are where most real-world concord mistakes happen, because so many words sit between the true subject and its verb.
SSS / PPP concord
Relative clause A clause always introduced by a relative pronoun — who, which, that, whom, whose. E.g. “The students who know the history of KNUST…”
Working out the verb inside (or governed by) a relative clause follows six steps:

items: 1Identify the relative clause.
2Identify the relative pronoun (RP).
3Identify the antecedent — the noun that the RP replaces/refers back to.
4Determine the number of the antecedent.
5Determine the number of the relative pronoun (it takes the same number as its antecedent).
6Determine the number of the verb (singular or plural) to match.

blocks.x: SSS / PPP pattern Singular Antecedent + Singular Relative Pronoun + Singular Verb (SSS). Plural Antecedent + Plural Relative Pronoun + Plural Verb (PPP). The chain must match all the way through — a plural antecedent forces a plural ‘reading’ of the relative pronoun, which in turn forces a plural verb, however many words separate them.

Worked example — In-class assignment sentence Among the four options — “One of the students who read IT is here”, “One of the students who reads IT is here”, “One of the students who read IT are here”, “One of the students who reads IT are here” — the antecedent of ‘who’ is students (plural), so the relative-clause verb must be read (PPP), while the main-clause subject is One (singular), so the main verb must be is. The error-free option is: “One of the students who read IT is here.”
The headword formula

Complex subject formula (D) + (Pm1) + H + (Pm2) D = Determiner · Pm1 = Pre-modifier · H = Headword · Pm2 = Post-modifier. It is the Headword (H) — not the determiner, not any modifier — that determines the number of the verb.

Worked example “The newly elected first female Vice Chancellor of Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, who is a Professor in pharmaceutical sciences, relates well with all manner of people.” Despite the long stretch of pre- and post-modification, the headword is the singular Vice Chancellor, so the verb is the singular relates.
Simple subject
Always contains one word. Mathematics is my favourite subject.
Complex subject
Contains more than one word. The students from Togo are friendly.
Steps for dealing with a complex subject:

items: 1Identify the noun phrase that functions as the subject.
2Identify the headword of that noun phrase.
3Determine the number of the headword.
4Determine the number of the verb (singular or plural) to match the headword.

blocks.x: Two look-alike phrases, two different verbs

‘A number of’ vs. ‘The number of’ ‘A number of’ always requires a plural verb (it means “several,” so the focus is on the many items). ‘The number of’ selects a singular verb (the headword is ‘number’ itself, one figure). A number of the students know their rights, but the number of those who do not is very alarming.
Someone, everybody, anything — always singular

Most indefinite pronouns take singular verbs Built from one / body / thing: someone, somebody, something · anyone, anybody, anything · no one, nobody, nothing · everyone, everybody, everything. All of these are grammatically singular and take a singular verb, however plural they may feel in meaning.
Singular verb even with ‘and’

Each, many a, every, many an + and Use a singular verb when two or more subjects connected by ‘and’ are each preceded by each, many a, every, or many an. Every computer, printer, and fax machine is marked for sale. Many a woman and man has responded to our plea for voluntary donations.
Extended reference list

Important caution It is often said that these nouns ALWAYS require singular verbs, BUT their number is actually determined by the CONTEXT within which they are used. The politics in Ghana and Nigeria are (not “is”) different. SINGULAR: Statistics is a required course for undergraduate students. PLURAL: The statistics on female enrolment in our public universities are encouraging.
Causes of concord errors

items: 1Ignorance of the rules — some learners are simply unfamiliar with the general concord rules and their exceptions.
2Overgeneralization of rules — learners apply a rule everywhere without being aware of its exceptions.
3Forgetfulness — occurs when there are intervening words between the subject and the main verb, so the writer loses track of the subject's number.
4Difficulty distinguishing ‘grammatical’ and ‘pragmatic’ singular or plural subjects.
5Incomplete application of rules and plain carelessness.
6Ignorance of irregular plural/singular forms — words like phenomenon/phenomena, alumnus/alumnae, etc.

blocks.x: How to correct concord errors
Find the subject and the verb→ Ignore all intervening words→ Match verb number to subject number
In short: locate the true subject and its verb, ensure they agree, and ignore every intervening word between them — those words never affect agreement, no matter how close they sit to the verb.

items: “A number of the students know their rights.” → subject is “A number of the students,” headword idea is plural (“a number of” = several) → plural verb know is correct.
“The number of those who do not is very alarming.” → subject is “The number,” a singular headword → singular verb is is correct, even though “those who do not” sits right before it.
“Everybody in the hostels ___ (know/knows) the rules.” → “Everybody” is an indefinite pronoun → always singular → knows is correct, regardless of the intervening phrase “in the hostels.”
